title: The Turn of the Screw
author: Henry James
setting: Bly, an old family place in Essex, across one summer and autumn, with a Christmas-Eve frame in another old house
lengthNote: A prologue and twenty-four short chapters; the governess who writes most of it is never named
openingLine: The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless, but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome, as, on Christmas Eve in an old house, a strange tale should essentially be, I remember no comment uttered till somebody happened to say that it was the only case he had met in which such a visitation had fallen on a child.
summary: A young woman takes charge of two orphaned children in a country house on the condition that she never trouble their guardian about anything. She begins to see a man on a tower and a woman by a lake, learns from the housekeeper that both are dead, and concludes that they have come back for the children. Whether that conclusion is a rescue or the thing the children need rescuing from is the question James spends twenty-four chapters refusing to answer.
referenceStyle: chapter, with the frame narrative given as Prologue

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Turn of the Screw
sourceText.note: The frame is headed Prologue; the governess's manuscript runs in unheaded chapters numbered I to XXIV, and references here use those numerals.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: In Collier's Weekly, before its book appearance.

atAGlance.label: First collected
atAGlance.note: Printed with Covering End, a comedy in James's other register entirely.

atAGlance.label: Narrators
atAGlance.note: An unnamed guest reports Douglas, who reads a manuscript by a governess who is also not named.

atAGlance.label: The condition
atAGlance.note: The guardian's one requirement is the plot: no adult with authority can be consulted about anything that happens.

structure.label: Prologue
structure.title: Christmas Eve, and a manuscript in a locked drawer
structure.summary: Guests at a country house are trading ghost stories when Douglas offers one he has kept to himself for years. He has to send to town for the manuscript, which delays the telling by two nights, and he dies before the outer narrator makes the copy the reader is holding.

scenes.summary: A story about a child prompts Douglas to promise one about two.
A young clergyman's daughter answers an advertisement in Harley Street and accepts a post nobody else will take.
She promises never to appeal to her employer about anything, and never sees him again.

structure.label: Chapters I-IV
structure.title: Bly, two beautiful children, and a man on the tower
structure.summary: The governess arrives to find Flora enchanting, Mrs Grose welcoming and the house larger than she expected. A letter says Miles has been expelled and gives no reason; she decides to ask nobody. Twice she sees a strange man, once on the tower and once looking in through the dining-room window.

scenes.summary: First evening at Bly, and a place that seems to her like a great drifting ship.
The school's letter is burned in conversation rather than answered.
Miles arrives; at the end of her own hour a figure appears at the top of the tower.
The same man looks in at a window, and the governess goes out to take his place at the glass.

structure.label: Chapters V-VIII
structure.title: The housekeeper names two of the dead
structure.summary: From the governess's description, Mrs Grose identifies Peter Quint, a former valet who is dead, and then Miss Jessel, the previous governess, also dead. What Mrs Grose actually says about the pair is much less than what the governess takes from it, and the difference between the two is the engine of the rest of the book.

scenes.summary: The description is given, and Mrs Grose's face finishes it.
Quint was too free with the boy; the governess decides she is a screen between the children and the dead.
A woman in black across the lake, seen while Flora plays with her back to the water.
Mrs Grose is pressed on what she knew and admits she said nothing at the time.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XIV
structure.title: Night stairs, and children who are never caught
structure.summary: The governess keeps watch by night and finds Quint on the staircase, Miss Jessel on the stair below, Flora at the window and Miles on the lawn looking up. Every incident is explained away charmingly by one child or the other, and she begins to read the charm itself as the proof.

scenes.summary: A figure on the staircase in the small hours, met without a candle.
Flora is found at the window; Miles admits he was out on the lawn to be, for once, bad.
The governess reconstructs the night with Mrs Grose in the daylight.
She concludes that the children belong to the dead and always have.
Weeks of unspoken watching, in which nobody names anything.
Miles, walking to church, asks when he is to go back to school.

structure.label: Chapters XV-XXI
structure.title: A letter, a lake, and Flora sent away
structure.summary: The governess writes to the guardian at last, finds Miss Jessel at her own schoolroom desk, and takes Mrs Grose to the lake to force Flora into an admission. Flora sees nothing, turns on her, and is taken to London the next morning; the letter never left the house.

scenes.summary: Miss Jessel is found in the schoolroom and addressed aloud.
The governess agrees to write to the children's uncle.
A night scene at Miles's bedside, ended by a gust that blows out the candle.
Miles plays the piano while Flora slips out of the house.
The search leads to the lake, where the boat has been moved.
The governess names Miss Jessel across the water; Flora sees nothing and asks to be taken away.
Mrs Grose reports Flora's new vocabulary, and the letter is found to have been stolen.

structure.label: Chapters XXII-XXIV
structure.title: Alone in the house with Miles
structure.summary: With Flora and Mrs Grose gone, the governess sets out to get a confession over a dish of mutton. Miles admits he said things at school; the white face appears at the window; and in getting the name out of him she is holding a child whose heart has stopped.

scenes.summary: The house's servants stare, and dinner is served downstairs like a trial.
Miles asks to be let alone and is not.
The confession, the figure at the glass, and the last three words of the book.

characters.name: The governess
characters.role: Twenty years old, a country parson's youngest daughter, in her first post
characters.summary: She writes the account, so every fact in it has already passed through her. She is brave, observant and entirely alone with a responsibility she has promised not to share, and the novella gives the reader no instrument for telling her courage apart from her certainty.
characters.clue: She takes a post on condition that she never write to her employer, and then never does, even when she has a reason that would justify it.

characters.name: Mrs Grose
characters.summary: She cannot read, which means every written thing at Bly passes through the governess, and she knows the household's history but volunteers almost none of it. Her agreement is usually a repetition of what she has just been told, and the governess treats each repetition as independent evidence.
characters.clue: She keeps the keys and the past of the house, and has to ask somebody else to read her letters.

characters.name: Miles
characters.role: Ten years old, sent down from school
characters.summary: Expelled for something the school will not put in writing and he will not put into words, he is courteous, oddly adult and perfectly capable of managing the woman in charge of him. The single thing he finally admits, that he said things to boys he liked, is small enough to be anything at all.
characters.clue: A boy of ten who cannot go back to school, plays the piano to cover his sister's escape, and dies at the moment he gives up a name.

characters.name: Flora
characters.summary: For half the book she is the most charming child in English fiction and for one page she is something else, refusing to look where she is told to look and turning a face on the governess that the narrative calls hard. She is removed to London and never gets to give her account.
characters.clue: She shows a new governess round a house like a small chatelaine, and later begs to be taken away from her.

characters.name: Peter Quint
characters.role: The master's former valet, dead before the story begins
characters.summary: Described before he is named, in a passage of clothes and hair and a habit of going bareheaded, and identified by a housekeeper who has heard the description rather than seen the man. He died on the ice coming back from a public house, and everything else said about him at Bly is inference.
characters.clue: He wore his master's waistcoats without permission and was found dead on a road one winter morning.

characters.name: Miss Jessel
characters.role: The previous governess, dead before the story begins
characters.summary: She left Bly and died, and the reason is given only in hints that the present governess completes for herself. Seen in black across the lake and at the schoolroom desk, she is the position the narrator currently occupies, which is a large part of why she is so frightening.
characters.clue: She sat at this desk before, left in the middle of a summer, and is seen again on the other side of the water.

characters.name: The master
characters.role: The children's uncle, in Harley Street
characters.summary: Handsome, busy and entirely offstage after the prologue, he creates the conditions of the story by refusing to be part of it. His prohibition removes the one person who could confirm or dismiss anything the governess believes, and she keeps to it long after keeping to it has stopped making sense.
characters.clue: He is handsome, lives in London, and requires only that nobody ever tell him anything.

characters.name: Douglas
characters.role: The reader of the manuscript, in the frame
characters.summary: He knew the governess when he was an undergraduate and she was his sister's governess, kept her manuscript in a locked drawer for years, and admits she was in love with her employer before he begins. He dies soon afterwards and sends the papers to the narrator, so the text arrives with its witness already gone.
characters.clue: He keeps a story in a locked drawer for forty years and has to send to town for it before he can tell it.
traits: dead before the account is copied

themes.name: Evidence and the single witness
themes.summary: Nobody else in the story ever sees an apparition. The governess's proof is that Mrs Grose recognises a description, and Mrs Grose is being asked to recognise it after being told what to expect. James keeps the reader in exactly the position of a juror with one witness and no corroboration, and then stops.
themes.development: Corroboration in Chapter V feels total; by Chapter XX, when Flora looks at an empty stretch of water, the same procedure produces nothing at all.

themes.name: Innocence and what adults do with it
themes.summary: The children's beauty is described in religious terms and then read as a disguise, and the reading comes first: the governess decides what she is looking for and then finds the children charming in a way that confirms it. Whatever is wrong at Bly, the adults' certainty about it is doing measurable harm by the last chapter.
themes.development: A passion of tenderness in Chapter III, a theory of possession in Chapter XII, and a boy held to his confession until his heart stops in Chapter XXIV.

themes.name: The unsaid
themes.summary: Nothing in this book is ever specified. The school will not state Miles's offence, Mrs Grose will not describe what Quint did, and the governess repeatedly decides that naming a thing would be worse than leaving it. James makes the reader supply the content, which is why no two readers frighten themselves in quite the same way.
themes.development: A letter that gives no reason, a housekeeper who says only that Quint was too free, and a confession that amounts to saying things to boys who liked him.

themes.name: Class, service and who may speak
themes.summary: Everyone at Bly is somebody's employee, and the horror is organised by rank: a valet who wore his master's waistcoats, a governess who is neither family nor servant, a housekeeper who cannot read, and a master who has purchased the right not to be told. Quint's real offence, as Bly describes it, is a matter of position before it is anything else.
themes.development: The prohibition in the Prologue, the too-free valet in Chapter VI, and the schoolroom desk that two women occupy in turn.

themes.name: Possession, influence and rescue
themes.summary: The governess understands herself as standing between the children and the dead, a screen, a shield, the one person who will act. That self-description is heroic and also exactly what a frightening adult would say, and the story ends with the rescue and the fatality being the same gesture.
themes.development: The screen in Chapter VI, the demons in Chapter XII, and the embrace in Chapter XXIV that is both a saving grip and the thing that kills.

themes.name: The frame, and how a story gets to us
themes.summary: Three narrators and a forty-year delay stand between the reader and Bly. The manuscript is in a locked drawer, its keeper is in love with its author, and by the time it is copied out both of them are dead, so the text arrives with every route back to a fact closed off.
themes.development: Douglas promises a second turn of the screw in the Prologue and then dies; the novella never returns to the fire, and no outer narrator comments at the end.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, by a narrator with his own interests.
techniques.inThisBook: The Christmas-Eve frame gives the story a title, a delay, a champion for the governess and, crucially, no way of checking her: it closes without returning to the fireside.

techniques.name: Withheld specifics
techniques.definition: Refusing to name the act, the word or the offence that the plot turns on.
techniques.inThisBook: Miles's expulsion, Quint's freedom and Miss Jessel's disgrace are all left as gaps, and readers fill them with material James never supplied.

techniques.name: Suspended syntax
techniques.definition: Sentences that qualify themselves clause by clause before reaching the verb that matters.
techniques.inThisBook: The governess's prose delays its own conclusions with dashes and parentheses, so that the reader experiences her habit of thought as much as her account of events.

techniques.name: The reported sighting
techniques.definition: An apparition given only as one person's report, never as an event the narrative confirms.
techniques.inThisBook: James never writes that Quint is there; he writes that she saw him, and the difference is the whole argument between a century of readings.

techniques.name: Leading questions
techniques.definition: Producing testimony by supplying the answer inside the question.
techniques.inThisBook: Mrs Grose is asked whether the man had no hat, and Flora is asked where Miss Jessel is; one witness agrees and one does not, by the same method.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Pairing characters so that one occupies another's position.
techniques.inThisBook: Two governesses at one desk, two children, two dead servants, and a title that promises a second turn of a screw already turned once.

quotations.text: The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless, but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome, as, on Christmas Eve in an old house, a strange tale should essentially be, I remember no comment uttered till somebody happened to say that it was the only case he had met in which such a visitation had fallen on a child.
quotations.context: The opening sentence, in the voice of the outermost narrator.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a hundred words long and arrives at its subject, a child, only at the very end, which is the book's method in miniature. Note also that the first thing we are told about the story we are about to read is that it is not the one being told.

quotations.text: If the child gives the effect another turn of the screw, what do you say to two children
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Offering his story in answer to one about a single haunted child.
quotations.analysis: The title is produced as a piece of after-dinner arithmetic: horror treated as a quantity that can be doubled. It also sets the terms on which everything that follows will be judged, because a story introduced as an intensification has to deliver one.

quotations.text: The story won’t tell
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Asked whether the story will say what the governess felt for her employer.
quotations.analysis: He is answering a question about motive, and the refusal is attributed to the manuscript rather than to himself. James thus establishes in the frame that the document is capable of not telling, and readers are warned before the first chapter that omission here is deliberate.

quotations.text: That she should never trouble him⁠—but never, never: neither appeal nor complain nor write about anything; only meet all questions herself, receive all moneys from his solicitor, take the whole thing over and let him alone.
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Describing the one condition attached to the post, which several other applicants had refused.
quotations.analysis: Every verb in the list is one the governess is forbidden to perform, and the accumulation makes the prohibition sound like a courtesy. The plot that follows is simply this sentence being kept: there is no adult she is permitted to consult, and she never breaks it.

quotations.text: He was incredibly beautiful, and Mrs. Grose had put her finger on it: everything but a sort of passion of tenderness for him was swept away by his presence.
quotations.context: Meeting Miles at the inn, the day after the school's letter arrives.
quotations.analysis: She decides the charge against him is impossible on the evidence of his face, and says so before she has asked him a single question. The verb swept away is worth keeping: her judgement of Miles is described from the start as something that happens to her rather than something she does.

quotations.text: Someone would appear there at the turn of a path and would stand before me and smile and approve.
quotations.context: Her habitual daydream during the free hour she takes in the grounds before dark.
quotations.analysis: This is the wish that the first apparition answers, and James puts it on the page a paragraph before Quint appears. The man she wants is the employer she has promised not to write to, so the figure on the tower arrives in a space her own longing has already prepared.

quotations.text: What arrested me on the spot⁠—and with a shock much greater than any vision had allowed for⁠—was the sense that my imagination had, in a flash, turned real.
quotations.context: The instant she catches sight of a man at the top of the tower.
quotations.analysis: The phrasing is doing two incompatible jobs at once: an imagination turning real is either a ghost or a symptom, and the sentence commits to neither. Almost every sighting in the book is worded with the same care.

quotations.text: So I saw him as I see the letters I form on this page
quotations.context: Insisting on the clarity of the first sighting.
quotations.analysis: She guarantees the apparition by comparing it with her own handwriting, which is the only thing the reader actually has. The comparison is meant as proof and works as a warning: everything we can see is the writing.

quotations.text: Quint was much too free.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Grose
quotations.context: Explaining why the valet was so often with the boy.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and they are the entire documented case against Peter Quint. Free is a word about rank as much as conduct, and the governess converts it into something much larger over the following chapters without ever being given more.

quotations.text: He was looking for little Miles.
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Concluding what Quint wanted when he looked in at the window.
quotations.analysis: She calls this a portentous clearness, and it is the first time she states a motive for an apparition rather than a fact about one. From here the sightings stop being events to be explained and become moves in a campaign she believes she has understood.

quotations.text: I was a screen⁠—I was to stand before them. The more I saw, the less they would.
quotations.context: Working out what her role in the household now is.
quotations.analysis: The image makes her heroism and her monopoly the same thing: standing in front of the children means standing between them and any other account of what is happening. The arithmetic in the second sentence is stated as a certainty and never once tested.

quotations.text: They’re not mine⁠—they’re not ours. They’re his and they’re hers!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Telling Mrs Grose what she has concluded about the children's good behaviour.
quotations.analysis: The children's goodness has been reinterpreted as evidence against them, which means no conduct of theirs can now count in their favour. Possession is stated grammatically, in four possessive pronouns, and the sentence takes them away from Mrs Grose as well.

quotations.text: For the love of all the evil that, in those dreadful days, the pair put into them. And to ply them with that evil still, to keep up the work of demons, is what brings the others back.
quotations.context: Answering Mrs Grose's question about why the dead should return.
quotations.analysis: Demons is the point at which her vocabulary leaves the household and enters theology, and the others is the phrase she now uses for people she has named. Once the case is put in these terms, any intervention at all can be justified as rescue.

quotations.text: You terrible, miserable woman!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Finding a figure seated at her own desk in the schoolroom.
quotations.analysis: She has just recorded the extraordinary chill of feeling that she was the intruder, and the outburst is what that feeling turns into. Both women have sat at this desk in charge of these children, which is why the insult lands so close to home.

quotations.text: She’s there, she’s there!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: At the lake, seizing Mrs Grose's arm and pointing across the water at Flora's back.
quotations.analysis: This is the one moment when the apparition is put to a public test, in daylight, with two other people present. Neither of them sees anything, and the governess's response is not doubt but a louder assertion, which tells the reader what kind of proof she is now capable of accepting.

quotations.text: Take me away, take me away⁠—oh, take me away from her!
quotations.speaker: Flora
quotations.context: Buried in Mrs Grose's skirts, moments after being asked where Miss Jessel is.
quotations.analysis: The child's only sustained utterance in the book is a plea to be removed from her protector, and the pronoun at the end is unambiguous. Whatever else is at Bly, this is the sentence the reader has to place any reading of the governess against.

quotations.text: I could only get on at all by taking “nature” into my confidence and my account, by treating my monstrous ordeal as a push in a direction unusual, of course, and unpleasant, but demanding, after all, for a fair front, only another turn of the screw of ordinary human virtue.
quotations.context: Steadying herself before dinner on the first day alone with Miles.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for the title herself, and applies it not to the horror but to her own endurance, as though virtue were a thing that could be tightened. The phrase quietly admits that what she is about to do to a ten-year-old is an extremity rather than a duty.

quotations.text: For there again, against the glass, as if to blight his confession and stay his answer, was the hideous author of our woe⁠—the white face of damnation.
quotations.context: The figure appears at the window just as Miles begins to answer her.
quotations.analysis: The apparition arrives precisely when a confession is about to be completed, which is convenient for the reading that it is a projection and equally convenient for the reading that it is a rival. James supplies no third possibility and no narrator to adjudicate.

quotations.text: Peter Quint⁠—you devil!
quotations.speaker: Miles
quotations.context: His answer when asked whom he means by 'he'.
quotations.analysis: The line can be read two ways with no change of wording: the devil is either Quint at the window or the woman holding him. The governess takes it as her triumph and calls it his supreme surrender of the name, which is a phrase about an interrogation rather than a haunting.

quotations.text: We were alone with the quiet day, and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: Dispossessed is the governess's word and it claims a success: the demon has been evicted. Placed between two commas in a sentence that ends with stopped, it also reads as the cause of death, and James lets both meanings stand without a syllable of comment from anyone outside her account.

timeline.label: Henry James born in New York
timeline.detail: Into a family that moved repeatedly between America and Europe throughout his childhood.

timeline.label: James settles in London
timeline.detail: He spent most of the rest of his life in England and became a British subject in 1915.

timeline.label: Guy Domville fails at the St James's Theatre
timeline.detail: James was booed at his own curtain call and abandoned writing for the stage; the fiction of the following years is markedly more compressed and dramatic.

timeline.label: What Maisie Knew published
timeline.detail: Another book built on a child's partial understanding of adults, written immediately before this one.

timeline.label: Serialised in Collier's Weekly
timeline.detail: The story reached its first readers in a popular illustrated weekly rather than a literary quarterly.

timeline.label: Collected in The Two Magics
timeline.detail: Published with Covering End, so that the ghost story shared a volume with a comedy.

timeline.label: Revised for the New York Edition
timeline.detail: James reworked the text and added a preface discussing how the story was made.

timeline.label: James dies in London
timeline.detail: He had taken British nationality the previous year, during the war.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres in Venice
timeline.detail: The Turn of the Screw set for chamber orchestra, with Quint written for a tenor who sings, which the novella's Quint never does.

timeline.label: The Innocents released
timeline.detail: Jack Clayton's film, with Deborah Kerr as the governess and a screenplay that keeps the ambiguity deliberately open.

places.name: Harley Street, London
places.note: The guardian's house, where the governess is interviewed and gives her promise.

places.name: Essex
places.note: Bly is described only as an old family place in Essex; James names no town and draws no map.

places.name: De Vere Gardens, Kensington
places.note: James's London flat through the 1890s, the years of Maisie and this story.

places.name: Rye, East Sussex
places.note: Lamb House, where James lived and worked for the last phase of his career.

places.name: New York
places.note: James's birthplace, and the city whose collected edition he revised the story for in 1908.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading, and the one the text supports most directly: a governess of ordinary good sense describes a man she has never seen or heard of, and a housekeeper who knew him recognises him from the description.
criticalViews.counter: Mrs Grose is told a great deal before she confirms anything, and no second person ever sees a figure at any point in the story.

criticalViews.position: The apparitions are the governess's own
criticalViews.summary: A reading associated with Edmund Wilson and developed by much twentieth-century criticism, which treats the sightings as projections of a young woman's isolation, her feeling for her employer and her fear of what she has taken on.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain how she describes Quint's clothes and habits before anyone has told her about him, and it can make Flora's terror and Miles's death seem like a foregone conclusion rather than a horror.

criticalViews.summary: A third position holds that the story is built so that neither reading can win, and that James's preface and the frame narrative are both engineered to withhold the evidence a decision would need.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating a cruel and specific story about two children as a clever machine, and it can leave nothing to say about what actually happens at the lake.

essayQuestions.question: How does James make it impossible to decide whether the ghosts are real?
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, corroboration and the single witness
plan: Set out what a reader is actually given: one person's manuscript, copied after her death, with no outer narrator returning to comment.
Examine the identification of Quint in Chapter V closely, distinguishing what the governess supplies from what Mrs Grose supplies.
Contrast the lakeside scene in Chapter XX, where the same method is used in daylight and produces nothing.
Consider the wording of the sightings themselves, which report seeing rather than asserting presence.
Conclude on the frame: Douglas is in love with the author of the manuscript, and both are dead before it is copied.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of the children.
plan: Begin with the language of Chapter III, where beauty is described in religious terms and used as evidence.
Trace the reversal in Chapter XII, at which good behaviour becomes proof of corruption.
Use Flora's outburst at the lake and Miles's confession about saying things as the only direct evidence either child offers.
Weigh what Miles is actually accused of against what readers have traditionally supplied.
Decide what the last chapter shows: a child freed, or a child questioned to death.

essayQuestions.question: What does the prologue contribute to the story?
plan: Describe the layers: an unnamed guest, Douglas, a locked drawer, a manuscript, and a forty-year delay.
Show how the title is produced as a figure of speech about intensifying horror before the story begins.
Note what Douglas says and refuses to say about the governess's feelings for her employer.
Examine the master's condition as the plot's precondition rather than an item of background.
Consider the effect of never returning to the fireside: the story ends without anyone to receive it.

essayQuestions.question: 'The horror at Bly is a matter of class before it is a matter of ghosts.' Discuss.
plan: Establish everyone's position: master, governess, housekeeper, valet, and children who belong to none of them.
Read what is said about Quint, noting that the phrase used against him is about freedom rather than any named act.
Consider Mrs Grose's illiteracy, which puts every document in the house under the governess's control.
Set the two governesses at one desk beside each other, and ask what happened to the first.
Test the statement against the ending: Miles's expulsion concerns words said to other boys, and no adult will repeat them.

discussionQuestions: Nobody but the governess ever sees anything. Does that settle the question, or is it exactly what a ghost story requires?
Mrs Grose agrees with almost everything she is told. Is she a witness at all?
Miles is expelled for something the school will not name and he will barely describe. Why does James leave the gap open?
At the lake, Flora asks to be taken away from the governess. How much weight should a reader give that?
The story is told by three people and heard by none of them at the end. What does the missing return to the fireside do to the ending?

related.why: An earlier English novel assembled entirely from partial testimonies, and equally interested in who is allowed to be believed.
The other great governess narrative: a young woman alone in a large house with a secret she is not told and an employer she must not question.
The Christmas-Eve tradition the prologue is sitting in, gathered as a collection.
The other great turn-of-the-century ghost writer, and the opposite method: everything specified, dated and documented.
A near-contemporary American story told by a woman whose account of a room nobody else will credit.
